In addition to submitting a proposal for the commission structure on transactions within the United States made through non-App Store in-app purchase systems, Apple also filed a motion expressing its willingness to discuss a settlement with Epic Games. Details are as follows.

Apple may be open to a settlement

Apple earlier today submitted a proposal outlining its desire to be allowed to collect commissions on transactions completed through payment systems outside the App Store.

Around the same time Apple filed its documents, the U.S. Supreme Court denied Apple's application to stay the lower court proceedings while it appealed Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers' contempt finding against the company. Apple had previously been ordered by the court to allow developers to direct users to outside payment methods, yet it still chose to charge a 27% commission, resulting in the contempt ruling.

Under the structure proposed by Apple, it could charge up to a 15% commission on transactions completed through alternative payment systems. Epic Games immediately pushed back, stating that it "believes these fees fall well outside the Ninth Circuit's guidance on the range of permissible fees."

Although this document drew the most attention, Apple today also filed a separate motion requesting that Judge Gonzalez Rogers order both parties to attend a settlement conference.

From the content of the filing (edited for clarity):

This means that Apple's legal team had reached out to Epic's lawyers before filing the motion to discuss holding a settlement conference, but Epic did not agree to Apple's request.

Apple argued in its filing that the court has the power to order both parties to hold a settlement conference even without Epic's consent, adding that the Ninth Circuit itself also encourages both parties to reach an agreement on an appropriate commission for off-site links.

The company also stated that "discussing potential settlement solutions in a confidential, non-adversarial environment would increase the chances of reaching a pragmatic resolution, thereby avoiding lengthy remand proceedings."

It is worth noting that this filing does not include Apple's settlement proposal or terms, nor does it constitute a substantive settlement offer. What Apple is actually doing is requesting the court to order both parties to conduct settlement negotiations under the supervision of Magistrate Judge Joseph C. Spero.
